notes: First end-to-end column-transcriber test. Re-run after prior session's outputs were lost (not saved to disk). Sonnet recovered the small ads in order; correctly diagnosed unmasked ad and raised repair. Saved as part of the first comparison run on col0 of 1892-01-01 p1.

Comparison run alongside Sonnet. Haiku produced sparse output with fabrications (RAGS for FACTS, A. W. for A. H., PARSON'S for PAKENHAM, Seona for Scenes) and missed the unmasked-ad situation entirely. Sonnet is the production default.

First Opus direct transcript. User flagged that this contained conjectured body text — I had echoed Sonnet's reading of small print I could not actually resolve at the rendering I had. Superseded by v2 under updated agent rules.

Iteration 2 under updated agent rules (no fabrication clause + horizontal-rule markers). Transcribed only legibly-present text; marked all small-print body as [~N lines body text illegible] or [?…] for uncertain readings. Honest at the rendering I had — but the rendering was wrong: I was reading a downsampled view of the 911x8313 PNG and didn't realise the body text was actually present and readable. Superseded by v3 after slicing the column with PIL into six 1700px chunks at native res.

Iteration 3 — reading native-resolution chunks (/tmp/col0_chunk{0..5}.png at 1700px tall, 100px overlap, sliced with PIL from the 911x8313 column PNG). v1 and v2 were both reading a downsampled rendering; v1 fabricated body text, v2 honestly marked it illegible. v3 reads the actual text. Falsifications corrected: MACDONELL & STAFFORD (not Strawbridge), JAS. L. C. MORE (not Baskerville), JOHN SCOTT (not Roche), R. F. Nagle/PANMURE (not Haggart/Pakenham), W. J. Scott of WHITE LAKE (not Mitchell Lane), 20 CENTS EACH for new horse shoes (not 90), Tinware in Endless Variety (not Flowers). This is now the strict-diplomatic baseline. Major implication for dispatched agents: Sonnet/Haiku face the same downsampling problem unless tall columns are sliced before dispatch — the prompt's no-fabrication rule cannot save a model that can't actually see the text.

Phase A experiment, sliced mode. Column sliced at h-rules with 20px overlap into 12 slices via /tmp/phase_a_slice.py; manifest at transcribe/work/slices/<row>/manifest.json. Sonnet read each slice and emitted per-slice transcripts. RESULT: matches the Opus v3 benchmark on every previously-fabricated fact — MACDONELL & STAFFORD, JAS. L. C. MORE, JOHN SCOTT, R. F. NAGLE, PANMURE, WHITE LAKE, 20 CENTS EACH, Tinware in Endless Variety. Bonus signals: noted overlap bleed at slice edges and ignored it as instructed; flagged a within-slice h-rule the cutting stage missed (slice 9 above FACTS FOR ALL); flagged severe ink bleed/damage on slice 11. Minor artefacts: 'Phaeton' instead of 'Phæton' (æ ligature lost); 'Almonte, P.O.' vs 'Almonte. P.O.'. Conclusion: h-rule slicing fixes the downsampling-driven fabrication. Phase B wire-in is justified.

Phase A control — same Sonnet, same diplomatic-transcript instructions including no-fabrication clause, but reading the full 911x8313 PNG. Fabricated extensively despite the explicit instructions: 'T. P. PAIGE' for $5 REWARD signature (actual JAS. L. C. MORE), 'W. T. PAIGE' for store ad (actual R. F. NAGLE), 'WHITE LANE' (actual WHITE LAKE), '90 CENTS EACH' (actual 20), 'Flowers in Endless Variety, Stamped and Japanese Ware' (actual Tinware/Japanned Ware), garbled 'WEAV SIC, DOE DOOR' for the Crossley ad. The model honestly noted in transcriber_notes that it was working at downsampled resolution and could not read body text — yet still emitted plausible names where it could not read them. Confirms: the no-fabrication rule is necessary but not sufficient when the image is downsampled. Slicing is the structural fix.

Phase A second comparison — Haiku on the same 12 h-rule-bounded slices. RESULT: matches the Opus v3 benchmark on every previously-fabricated fact (MACDONELL & STAFFORD, JAS. L. C. MORE, JOHN SCOTT, R. F. NAGLE, PANMURE, WHITE LAKE, 20 CENTS EACH, Tinware/Japanned Ware). Slicing fixes the fabrication mode regardless of model. Quality differences vs Sonnet sliced: Haiku misread '$35.00' for the new Top Buggy where benchmark + Sonnet both have '$85.00' (single-digit OCR slip, 3 vs 8); missed the printed manicule ☞ in slices 4/6/8 and emitted '---' instead — would inject false rule markers if the orchestrator joined naively; did not flag the within-slice h-rule on slice 9 (above FACTS FOR ALL) that Sonnet caught; did not hedge the ambiguous '1[?b]' issue character at the masthead; included masthead 'Almonte.' bleed at top of slices 0 and 4 instead of ignoring the overlap as instructed. Bonus: preserved the Phæton ligature (Sonnet wrote 'Phaeton'). Net: Haiku is viable for clean structural facts on sliced inputs; Sonnet remains stronger on edge cases, hesitation markers, and printer's-mark recognition. Production default stays Sonnet; Haiku is a candidate for cheap-and-clean classified columns later.
